titleText.es: El veto de la UAI vino después del incidente
titleText.en: The IAU ban came after the 'redefinition of 'planet' to include the IAU president's mom' incident.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish archive metadata is truncated after incidente because the page places unescaped quotation marks inside its HTML title attribute. The page continues with the same invented planet-redefinition insult preserved in the complete official English title text; UAI is the Spanish abbreviation for the International Astronomical Union, called the IAU in English.

regions.labelEs: HOLA, SOY RANDALL. BIENVENIDOS A MI CHARLA TED.

excludedUnits.rationale: Randall is the speaker's unchanged personal name, not Spanish vocabulary.
TED is the unchanged proper name and acronym of the conference series, not Spanish lexical vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: SOIS ALGUNOS DE LOS INNOVADORES MÁS BRILLANTES, DE MUCHOS CAMPOS, ES UN HONOR HABLAROS DE UN PROBLEMA QUE NECESITA DESESPERADAMENTE DE VUESTRA ATENCIÓN:

applications.explanationEn: Sois is the present form of ser for the several people addressed informally in the form used mainly in Spain.
Algunos selects a masculine or mixed subset, and de los introduces the larger group named by innovadores.
This de connects algunos to the larger group from which that subset is selected.
Los matches the plural group, innovadores names it, and más brillantes marks the highest degree of the description.
Problema names the thing being described, que links it to the added information, and necesita supplies the verb inside that description.
Es un honor introduces the respectful evaluation, and hablaros supplies the following action in its unchanged dictionary form.
Os is attached directly to the unchanged verb hablar and identifies the several people addressed.
The attached os refers to several people addressed informally, a form used mainly in Spain.
Desesperada takes the ending -mente to form a word describing the urgent manner or degree of the need.
This de introduces what is required after necesita; natural English absorbs the relationship into the verb ‘need’ or ‘require.’
Vuestra addresses several people informally and uses feminine singular agreement for the one feminine thing possessed.

regions.labelEs: ¿CÓMO CERRAR CON UN EMOTICONO UN ENUNCIADO ENTRE PARÉNTESIS?

applications.explanationEn: Cómo asks for the unknown method and keeps its written accent; cerrar stays in its unchanged -ar dictionary form.
Entre and paréntesis form the conventional writing expression for material placed between the two punctuation marks.

regions.labelEs: NO SE ME OCURRE UNA BUENA FORMA.

applications.exampleEs: SE ME OCURRE UNA BUENA FORMA
applications.explanationEn: Se marks the come-to-mind pattern, me identifies the person receiving the idea, ocurre agrees with one idea, and una buena forma fills that idea slot.

applications.explanationEn: Parece reports an impression, while descompensado y raro coordinate two masculine singular descriptions of the displayed option.

regions.labelEs: CONFERENCIAS EN LAS QUE ESTOY VETADO

applications.explanationEn: En supplies the relationship required by the later ban, las matches the feminine plural conferencias, and que links back to them.
This en is kept before las que because it introduces the events where the ban applies; natural English commonly uses ‘from.’
Las matches the feminine plural conferencias referred to by the relative expression.
Estoy presents the speaker's current state, and vetado is the masculine singular completed-action form describing that state.

excludedUnits.rationale: SIGGRAPH is the unchanged proper name and acronym of a conference, not Spanish vocabulary.
EUROCRYPT is the unchanged proper name of a conference, not Spanish vocabulary.
DEFCON is the unchanged proper name of a conference, not Spanish vocabulary.
PyCon is the unchanged proper name of a conference, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Unión comes first, followed by the two descriptions astronómica and internacional in the common neutral order.
Astronómica uses feminine singular -a to match unión; internacional already has one singular form for both genders.
Conferencia names the event, and canadiense follows it as the description in the common neutral order.
Canadiense matches the feminine singular conferencia but uses the same singular form with masculine nouns.
Convenciones names the gatherings, and the borrowed describing word furry follows that noun.
The plural appears on convenciones; the borrowed adjective furry is used unchanged here rather than taking a Spanish plural ending.
Sociedad names the organization, and repostera follows it as the description in the common neutral order.
Repostera uses feminine singular -a to match the feminine singular noun sociedad.
Convención names the gathering, and asiática follows it as the description in the common neutral order.
Asiática uses feminine singular -a to match the feminine singular noun convención.

cards.answerEn: welcome (addressing a mixed or all-male group)
cards.noteEn: Bienvenidos is the masculine plural form of bienvenido. Use bienvenidas for an all-female group.
Charla can mean a spoken presentation for an audience. That is distinct from its conversational sense, where it means an informal chat or discussion.

example.es: Marta dio una charla sobre astronomía.
example.en: Marta gave a talk about astronomy.

cards.answerEn: you all are (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Sois is the present form of ser used with vosotros or vosotras, the informal way to address several people in Spain.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.questionEn: How do you say ‘some of’ a named group?
cards.answerEn: Use algunos or algunas, then de, then los or las and the group.
cards.noteEn: Choose algunos before a masculine or mixed set and algunas before a feminine set. Los or las agrees with the larger group that follows. This pattern selects a smaller set from that larger group.

cards.answerEn: of; links ‘some’ to the larger group
cards.noteEn: After algunos or algunas, de introduces the group from which the smaller set is chosen. Spanish normally keeps the matching article before that group: algunos de los, algunas de las.

example.es: Algunas de las ventanas están abiertas.
example.en: Some of the windows are open.

cards.questionEn: How do you describe someone or something as the most of a quality?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of “the,” name the person or thing, then add más plus the describing word.
cards.noteEn: The opening el, la, los, or las agrees with the noun. Más stays unchanged, while the final adjective changes when Spanish normally requires agreement.
Más normally means “more.” After el, la, los, or las, it can instead mark the highest degree in a group: la más rápida means “the fastest one.”
Brillante can describe a bright light or, figuratively, a very intelligent or impressive person. Its plural is brillantes for every gender.
Campo can mean a physical field, but in an academic context it means an area of knowledge or study. Campos is its plural.

example.es: La historia y la química son campos distintos.
example.en: History and chemistry are different fields.

cards.noteEn: Spanish can begin an impersonal evaluation with es plus a describing word. English normally supplies an impersonal ‘it,’ but Spanish does not add a separate subject word.

example.en: It is strange that it is raining.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that doing something is an honor?
cards.answerEn: Use es un honor, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, such as hablar, conocer, or recibir. Es can change when the time changes, but the action verb after honor stays in that dictionary form.

example.en: It is an honor to meet you.

cards.answerEn: to speak to you all (informal plural, mainly in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Hablaros joins hablar, the unchanged dictionary form meaning ‘to speak,’ with os, the short word for several people addressed informally in Spain.

example.en: I want to speak to you all about an idea.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.noteEn: Desesperadamente describes how an action is done. It is formed from the feminine singular describing form desesperada plus -mente.

example.en: He was desperately looking for the keys.

cards.questionEn: How do you turn many describing words into words such as “quickly,” “clearly,” or “probably”?
cards.answerEn: Use the feminine singular form of the describing word and add -mente. If its masculine and feminine forms are identical, simply add -mente.
cards.noteEn: For an adjective that changes, use its -a form: claro becomes clara and then claramente. For one form shared by both genders, probable becomes probablemente. The new word usually describes how an action happens or how the speaker judges a claim.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; a required verb complement
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

cards.answerEn: your (informal plural in Spain; before one feminine thing)
cards.noteEn: Vuestra says that something belongs to several people addressed informally. Its feminine singular ending matches the one feminine thing owned, not the number or gender of the owners.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what, how, or where to do something without naming a new person who does it?
cards.answerEn: Use an accented question word, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. This compact pattern is used when the person who would perform the action is already clear from context. The question word keeps its written accent even inside a larger statement: qué hacer, cómo llegar, dónde aparcar.

example.en: I do not know where to park.

cards.questionEn: Why can a parenthetical statement ending in an emoticon look ambiguous?
cards.answerEn: One closing parenthesis can look like both the smile's mouth and the end of the parenthetical text; adding another clarifies the structure but can make the face look odd.
cards.noteEn: The two rejected versions trade grammatical clarity against visual balance. The joke treats this tiny punctuation problem as an urgent topic for a prestigious talk.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that text is written in parentheses?
cards.noteEn: Entre usually means ‘between,’ but this conventional expression describes words placed between an opening and a closing parenthesis. Paréntesis has the same written form for one parenthesis and for more than one.
Paréntesis is written the same way in singular and plural. Context words reveal the number: un paréntesis is one parenthesis, while dos paréntesis is two parentheses.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the ‘come to mind’ use of ocurrir
cards.noteEn: In the pattern se me/te/le/nos/os/les ocurre, se is required before the short word naming the person who has the idea. It does not mean that the idea acts on itself.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an idea occurs to someone or comes to mind?
cards.answerEn: Put se before me, te, le, nos, os, or les, then use ocurre for one idea or ocurren for several.
cards.noteEn: The short word after se identifies who has the idea: me for me, te for informal you, le for one other person or formal you, nos for us, os for informal plural you in Spain, and les for several other people. The verb agrees with the idea, not with that person: ocurre una idea but ocurren dos ideas.
With se and a short recipient word such as me or le, ocurre presents an idea as coming to someone rather than simply reporting that an event happens.
Buena is the feminine singular form of bueno. It is used before or after a feminine singular noun, such as práctica or decisión.
Sería is the “would” form of ser, “to be.” Spanish keeps the full dictionary form ser and adds -ía.

example.en: It would be a good solution.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something seems to have a quality or state?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of parecer followed by the describing word.
cards.noteEn: The description agrees with the person or thing: parece cansado, parece cansada, parecen cansados. This reports an impression rather than asserting the state as a fact.
The prefix des- reverses compensado here: the parts no longer look balanced or well matched.

example.en: The drawing ended up looking unbalanced.

cards.answerEn: from; at (introducing where a ban applies)
cards.noteEn: After estar vetado, en introduces the place, event, or setting where the ban applies. Natural English often uses ‘from’ or ‘at’ rather than the usual literal ‘in.’

example.en: He is banned from several stadiums.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the feminine plural article inside las que (‘which’)
cards.noteEn: After a preposition, las can join que to refer back to feminine plural things. Las matches those things; que itself does not change.

example.es: Son las salas en las que trabajamos.
example.en: They are the rooms that we work in.

cards.answerEn: I am (in a state or condition)

cards.promptEs: estar + forma de acción completada que describe un estado
cards.questionEn: How do you describe the state something is in as the result of an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by the action's completed form, with an ending that matches the thing being described.
cards.noteEn: The completed form, often ending in -ado or -ido, is also called a participle. Estar changes for who or what is in the state. The participle changes like a describing word: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas. This pattern focuses on the resulting state, not on who performed the action.
Vetado is the masculine singular completed-action form of vetar. After estar, it describes the resulting state of being barred.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Canadiense has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
Here convención means an organized event or gathering. The same word can also mean an agreed practice or rule, which is a different sense.

example.es: La ciudad recibe varias convenciones cada año.
example.en: The city hosts several conventions each year.

cards.answerEn: furry; related to fans of anthropomorphic animal characters
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly borrows the English word furry for this subculture. When it modifies an event or group, it is often left unchanged for gender and number.

example.es: Hay una convención furry este fin de semana.
example.en: There is a furry convention this weekend.

cards.noteEn: EEUU abbreviates Estados Unidos. The repeated E and U show that both words are plural; formal writing often adds periods and a space as EE. UU.

example.es: La empresa vende sus productos en EEUU.
example.en: The company sells its products in the US.

cards.noteEn: Repostera can describe something connected with making cakes, pastries, and other sweets. Its feminine ending matches a feminine singular noun.
